topic: Binary Counting and the Towers of Hanoi: The Hidden Logic
target_audience: High school students or introductory CS students

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Binary Language
sections.content: Introduce binary (base-2) counting as a system using only 0 and 1. Explain that each digit position represents a power of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8...). Visualize this as a row of lightbulbs, where each bulb is either OFF (0) or ON (1).

sections.title: The Towers of Hanoi Challenge
sections.content: Introduce the puzzle: 3 rods and N disks of different sizes. Rules: 1 disk at a time, no larger disk on a smaller one. Define the goal: Move the stack from source to target. State the objective: How many moves are needed for N disks?
sections.example: A mechanical robot arm trying to move a 3-disk tower: Disk 1 (small), Disk 2 (medium), Disk 3 (large).

sections.title: Unveiling the Connection: Bitwise Movement
sections.content: Show that the number of moves follows the pattern 2^n - 1. Explain the deep link: each move in the sequence corresponds to the binary representation of the step number. Specifically, for any step 'k', the disk that moves is the position of the lowest set bit in the binary form of 'k'.
sections.example: For 3 disks, step 1 is '001' (disk 1 moves), step 2 is '010' (disk 2 moves), step 3 is '011' (disk 1 moves).

sections.title: Visualizing the Algorithm
sections.content: Use a graphical animation flow: As the binary counter increments (000 -> 001 -> 010 -> 011), map the bit changes directly to the movement of the disks on screen. This transforms a complex puzzle into a simple mechanical counting task.
sections.example: An animation showing a binary counter ticking up alongside a digital puzzle solver; as the bits flip, the specific disks shift rods automatically.

sections.title: Conclusion and Real-World Scaling
sections.content: Summarize that binary is the 'hidden blueprint' of the Towers of Hanoi. Mention that this power-of-two growth is why the puzzle becomes impossible for large N (e.g., 64 disks would take billions of years), illustrating the concept of exponential complexity.
sections.example: Comparison: A snail moving disks at 1 second per move vs. the total age of the universe.
